analytic.title: Optimal Order Assignment Algorithms for Single-Rate Time-Driven AFAP Cyclic Executives

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In a recent survey, it was observed that the majority of the respondents to the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in considered systems answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered". Cyclic executives, though hardly addressed in contemporary text books, if at all, are therefore still in use in practice. Hence, there is a need for analysis techniques for these executives.

In earlier work, exact analysis for single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives, scheduling a given sequence of independent hard real-time polling tasks in single-processor systems, have been presented. Unlike the analysis for single-rate AFAP cyclic executives, the analysis for single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives depends on the order of the tasks in the cycle. In this paper, we present two optimal order assignment (OOA) algorithms for single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives. The first algorithm yields a schedulable order of tasks if and only if such an order exists. The second algorithm enhances the first by yielding an order that maximizes the cycle time of the executive, effectively maximizing energy efficiency or improving the average response times of background tasks.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: As described in [1], cyclic executives are generally used in defense military systems and traffic control systems to handle periodic tasks. Cyclic executives effectively execute hard realtime tasks in a continuous loop, in which every task appears at least once. Since the paper by C. Douglass Locke [2], in which it is concluded that the fixed-priority approach generally dominates the cyclic executive approach for hard real-time systems, the academic interest in cyclic executives has gradually decreased 1 . Accordingly, cyclic executives are mentioned in contemporary text books, such as [1], [4]- [6], but hardly addressed in detail. Despite the decreasing academic interest, cyclic executives are still in use, however. In a recent survey of 120 industry practitioners in the field of real-time embedded systems [7], it was observed that from the 97 respondents to the question which task scheduling policy/policies are used in the considered systems, 54.17% answered "static cycle/table driven/time-triggered". Availability of exact analysis for cyclic executives therefore remains desirable.

Earlier work [8] presented exact analysis for single-rate AFAP (as fast as possible) and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives and discussed their relative strength and weaknesses in terms of jitter, energy efficiency, and schedulability. Based on these criteria, the two cyclic executives turned out to be incomparable. On the one hand, a time-driven AFAP cyclic executive outperforms an AFAP cyclic executive when jitter and energy efficiency are considered. On the other hand, the AFAP cyclic executive dominates the time-driven AFAP cyclic executive from a schedulability perspective.

Whereas the worst-case analysis for single-rate AFAP cyclic executives is independent of the order of the tasks in the cycle, the worst-case analysis for single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives is not. In [9], a conjecture for an optimal order assignment (OOA) algorithm has been presented, which determines a schedulable order iff (i.e. if-and-only-if) one exists. That paper only presented a proof sketch of the conjecture, however.

In this paper, we provide a proof for that conjecture in [9] 2 . In addition, an enhanced OOA algorithm is presented (and proven), which improves on the OOA algorithm by providing an order that maximizes the cycle time of the executive for a system, effectively maximizing energy efficiency or improving the average response times of background tasks. Finally, a proof is presented for Theorem 3 in [8], stating that the AFAP cyclic executive dominates the time-driven AFAP cyclic executive from a schedulability perspective.
The remainder of this document is organized as follows.

In Section II, we present a basic real-time system model. In Section III, we provide a recap of the two basic single-rate cyclic executives considered, including their exact analysis. A basic OOA algorithm is the topic of Section IV and an enhanced OOA algorithm the topic of Section V. We briefly revisit the discussion concerning the relative strength and weaknesses of the single-rate AFAP and single-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executives, in particular schedulability, in Section VI. The document is concluded in Section VII.

div.head: II. A BASIC REAL-TIME SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We assume a hard real-time system S, a set E S of n sporadic (input) events e 1 , e 2 , . . . , e n , a set R S of n (output) responses r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r n to these events, and a 1-1 relationship between events and responses. Events are sporadic, i.e. each event e i is characterized by a minimal inter-arrival time WT S i . Each event-response tuple e i , r i is characterized by a relative best-case system deadline BD S i and a relative worst-case system deadline WD S i , where 0 ≤ BD S i ≤ WD S i ≤ WT S i . Hence, whenever an event e i occurs at time t, the hard realtime system S must provide a response r i in the interval
div.formula: [t + BD S i , t + WD S i ]
div.p: . Moreover, we assume a set T S of n independent polling tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , where task τ i senses event e i and provides response r i . Each task τ i is characterized by a best-case computation time BC i and a worst-case computation time WC i , where 0 < BC i ≤ WC i . The execution of a task is termed a job. A job of task τ i is denoted by ι i,k , with 0 ≤ k, i.e. the first job of τ i is denoted by ι i,0 . The computation time C i,k of every job ι i,k of task τ i shall be between BC i and WC i , i.e.
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n ∧ 0≤k BC i ≤ C i,k ≤ WC i .
div.p: Although tasks scheduled by a cyclic executive are typically assumed to be periodic [10], i.e. are typically assumed to be activated with a fixed inter-arrival time (or period), we do not make that assumption in this document. Similarly, we do not assume (worst-case and best-case) deadlines of tasks.

We assume that tasks are scheduled by cyclic executives, run non-preemptively and do not suspend themselves. The sequence of tasks executed in a cycle is assumed to be known statically. Moreover, we ignore scheduling overhead and system initialization. When a system S meets all its deadlines under a specific cyclic executive and a specific sequence of tasks, the system S is called schedulable under that cyclic executive and that sequence.
For ease of presentation and without loss of generality, the jobs of tasks in a cycle are assumed to be executed in the order of increasing index.

div.head: III. RECAP OF CYCLIC EXECUTIVES AND THEIR ANALYSIS
div.p: For (basic) cyclic executives, tasks can simply be implemented as procedures and executed within a loop. A singlerate cyclic executive essentially executes every task exactly once in a cycle.
As described in [8], best-case deadlines of a system S are met for a (basic) single-rate cyclic executive when
div.formula: ∀ 1≤i≤n BC i ≥ BD S i .(1)
div.p: Best-case analysis is therefore independent of a specific cyclic executive, and not considered any further in this document.

In the following subsections, the single-rate AFAP and single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives are briefly recapitulated, including their exact worst-case analysis. We start with an example system, which we will use in the remainder of the paper for illustration purposes.

div.head: C. Single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive
div.p: For a single-rate time-driven AFAP, a cycle is started by a timer. The sum of the worst-case computation times of all tasks shall be less than the inter-arrival time T S of the timer, otherwise the (worst-case) executions of the tasks do not 'fit' in a cycle, i.e.
div.formula: 1≤i≤n WC i ≤ T S .

div.head: IV. A BASIC OPTIMAL ORDER ASSIGNMENT ALGORITHM
div.p: The worst-case schedulability analysis for the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive is dependent on the order of the tasks in the cycle; see (4). As an example, system S I is schedulable for a task order {τ 3 , τ 1 , τ 2 }.

In this section, we first rewrite Theorem 2 to support an arbitrary, but fixed, order of tasks in a cycle. Next, we show that the example system S I is schedulable for task order {τ 3 , τ 1 , τ 2 }. We subsequently provide a theorem for an optimal task order assignment algorithm and a proof. We conclude with a remark about complexity of the algorithm and test.

div.head: C. A theorem and an OOA algorithm
div.p: We define an optimal order assignment (OOA) policy O for a set T S of tasks of a system S scheduled by means of a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive as an order assignment that will make S schedulable, iff such an order exists.

Theorem 3. (Conjecture 1 in [9]) Given a system S and a set of tasks T S , the OOA algorithm (Algorithm 1) determines a sequence task[] that contains every task of T S exactly once, for which S is schedulable under a single-rate time-driven cyclic executive, iff such a sequence exists.

The OOA algorithm populates the sequence task[] from the last to the first element. It exploits the property that the schedulability of a task is affected by the set of tasks scheduled before it, not by the order of such tasks.

The OOA algorithm (see Algorithm 1) uses an auxiliary set of tasks T S,U that have not been put in the sequence task[] yet. The set T S,U is initialized to T S at line 1. Line 2 introduces an auxiliary constant T S,min for the lower bound on the cycle time T S . Next, the algorithm populates the sequence task[] from the last to the first element (lines 3-13). At each iteration, it searches for a schedulable task from T S,U (lines [4][5][6][7][8][9][10][11]. When a schedulable task is found, its index is put at the proper place in the sequence (line 7), the task is removed from T S,U (line 8), and a next iteration is started. When no schedulable task is found (line 12), the algorithm returns unschedulable. When at each iteration a schedulable task is found, the algorithm returns schedulable (line 14) and a schedulable sequence task[].

div.head: D. Proof of the theorem
div.p: The proof consists of three steps. The first step maps the problem onto the classical problem of an optimal fixed-priority assignment of tasks on a single processor. The second step shows that the schedulability test in Theorem 2 is compatible with the conditions for applicability of Audsley's OPA (Optimal Priority Assignment) Algorithm [11]- [13]. The third step shows the similarity of the OOA and the OPA algorithm.

div.head: 1) Step 1: Mapping on an FP-assignment problem:
div.p: A single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive for a system S executes every task of the task set T S of S non-preemptively, in a fixed order, and exactly once in a cycle with a cycle-time T S . Now assume each task of T S (i) is assigned a priority corresponding with its index in the sequence, where a smaller index represents a higher priority, and (ii) has the same (fixed) inter-arrival time, equal to the cycle-time T S . With these task properties, we get an identical schedule with fixed-priority non-preemptive scheduling of T S with a synchronous release of tasks [14]. The OOA problem is therefore casted to an OPA problem for fixed-priority non-preemptive scheduling, with a one-to-one relationship between the index (in the sequence) and the priority of a task.

Step 2: Compatibility of Theorem 2 with OPA algorithm conditions: For the schedulability test of Theorem 2 to be compatible with the OPA algorithm, it must comply with the following three conditions [13]:

1) The schedulability of a task τ k may, according to the test, depend on any independent properties of tasks with priorities higher than k, but not on any properties of those tasks that depend on their relative priority ordering.

2) The schedulability of a task τ k may, according to the test, depend on any independent properties of tasks with priorities lower than k, but not on any properties of those tasks that depend on their relative priority ordering. 3) When the priorities of any two tasks of adjacent priority are swapped, the task being assigned the higher priority cannot become unschedulable according to the test, if it was previously schedulable at the lower priority. These conditions refer to properties of a task that are independent of its priority. As an example, worst-case computation times of tasks are typically independent of the priority of a task, whereas worst-case response times are typically highly dependent on its relative priority.
The schedulability test (4) for a system S in Theorem 2 has been rewritten to a test for a task τ i at index k on line 5, i.e.
div.formula: T S,min ≤ WD S i - ⎛ ⎝ τ j ∈T S,U \{τ i } (WCj -BCj) + WCi ⎞ ⎠ , (6
div.p: where T S,U \{τ i } represents the set of tasks that have not been assigned an index yet and will (c.q. may) be put earlier in the sequence task[]. All three conditions hold for the rewritten test (6) of Theorem 2, i.e. inspection of (6) shows that 1) The schedulability of a task τ k only depends on the worst-case and best-case computation times of tasks with a higher priority (i.e. a lower index), being properties that are independent of the their relative priority ordering (i.e. order in the sequence).

2) The schedulability of task τ k is independent of tasks with a lower priority (i.e. a higher index). 3) Swapping adjacent tasks τ i and τ j in the sequence (i.e. of adjacent priorities), will not make the task receiving a lower index (i.e. τ i ) in the sequence unschedulable, if it was previously schedulable, because the left hand side of the inequality in the test is a constant and the right hand side is monotonically non-increasing when an element of the set T S,U \ {τ i } is removed. 3) Similarity between OOA and OPA algorithm: Algorithm 2 presents the pseudo-code of the OPA algorithm. Algorithm 1 is clearly an instantiation of the OPA algorithm with the test (6).

div.p: Similar to the OPA algorithm, the OOA algorithm has a complexity O(n 2 ). At each iteration (of the inner loop), a schedulability test is applied, which has a complexity O(n).

div.head: V. AN ENHANCED OPTIMAL ORDER ASSIGNMENT
ALGORITHM
div.p: In the previous section, we presented two task orders for system S I that are both schedulable under a single-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executive, i.e. {τ 3 , τ 1 , τ 2 } in Section IV-B and {τ 3 , τ 2 , τ 1 } using the OOA-algorithm in Section IV-C. Although both task orders are schedulable, the former is clearly preferred given the larger value for the cycle time T SI it can achieve, i.e. 16 versus 15.

In this section, we present an enhanced OOA algorithm, that not only determines an order assignment to make a system S schedulable by means of a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, if such an order exists, but that also determines the maximum cycle time T S,max for which S is schedulable. We start by recapitulating the fraction of time that can be gained by a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive compared to a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive. We subsequently briefly explore the problem of determining a maximum cycle time. A theorem and an enhanced OOA algorithm subsequently presented, followed by a proof of correctness. We conclude with a remark about complexity of the algorithm and test.

div.p: The advantage of a larger cycle time T S follows from the following lemma [8].

div.head: B. A first informal exploration
div.p: Equation (3) provides a lower bound for the cycle time T S . This lower bound T S,min is also used in the test for a task τ i at index k on line 5 in Algorithm 1; see also (6). When the OOA algorithm finds a schedulable sequence task[] for T S,min , we may subsequently repeatedly increase T S,min to find the maximum cycle time for which the system S remains schedulable. Essentially, the proof in Section IV-D remains valid when we parameterize the OOA algorithm with a parameter for a specific cycle time T S that is equal to or larger than the lower bound T S,min .

As an improvement, the OOA algorithm can be encapsulated by a binary search, using T S,lwb = 1≤i≤n WC i as a lower bound and T S,upb = min 1≤i≤n WD S i -WC i as an upper bound on T S,max . This initial upper bound simply ignores the fact that best-case and worst-case computation time might be different. For our leading example system S I , we find T SI,upb = min 1≤i≤3 (WD SI i -WC i ) = min{20-3, 23-4, 25-8} = min{17, 19, 17} = 17. Assuming integral numbers for task and system characteristics, the encapsulating binary search algorithm gives rise to an increase of the complexity with a factor O log 2 T S,upb -T S,lwb , however. In the next subsection, we therefore present an enhanced OOA algorithm with the same complexity as the OOA algorithm.

div.head: D. Proof of the theorem
div.p: The proof is based on two auxiliary lemmas. Lemma 3. The E-OOA algorithm (Algorithm 3) is an optimal order assignment algorithm.

Proof. Follows directly from equivalence with the OOA algorithm (Algorithm 1). (The equivalence can be seen by noting that the OOA algorithm is an optimal order assignment algorithm, irrespective of the initial ordering of the tasks and therefore irrespective of which unassigned but schedulable task is assigned to each index.) Lemma 4. The E-OOA algorithm yields a fixed sequence task[], if a schedulable order exists.

div.p: Proof. We observe that whenever the E-OOA algorithm returns schedulable, the derived sequence task[] only depends on the order in which the tasks in T S,U are processed in lines 6-19. This is because the algorithm selects the (first) task τ i with the largest T S,U,max i . Hence, as long as the system S is schedulable by a sequence, the sequence returned by the algorithm is therefore always the same, independent of the value of T S,min .

Because the E-OOA algorithm (Algorithm 3) is an optimal order assignment algorithm (see Lemma 3), it will yield a schedulable sequence iff one exists. Because the E-OOA algorithm always yields the same sequence when a schedulable sequence exists (see Lemma 4), it will also yield that same sequence when T S,min is initialized to the largest T S,max . The E-OOA algorithm therefore returns a sequence task[] with the largest T S,max .

div.head: E. Concluding remark
div.p: Similar to the OOA algorithm, our E-OOA algorithm has a complexity O(n 2 ), and the schedulability test, which is applied in the inner-loop, has a complexity O(n).

In [15], a robust priority assignment (RPA) algorithm is presented, using an additional interference function E(α, w, i), that is required to be a monotonic non-decreasing function of its parameters. Given our mapping on an FP-assignment problem in Section IV-D1, an algorithm similar to RPA can be conceived for our problem by defining E(α, w, i) = T S,U,max i ; see line 8 of Algorithm 3. Because the RPA algorithm is based on binary search, the resulting algorithm would have a higher complexity than our E-OOA algorithm; see Section V-B.

div.head: VI. A COMPARISON BETWEEN BASIC CYCLIC EXECUTIVES
div.p: In this section, we compare single-rate AFAP and singlerate time-driven AFAP cyclic executives from a scheduling perspective. We first present a lemma stating that if a system is schedulable under a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, then it will also be schedulable under a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive. We subsequently present an example system that meets its worst-case deadlines under a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive, but is not schedulable by a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, not even when applying the OOA algorithm. We conclude the section with a theorem. Lemma 5. When a system S is schedulable under a singlerate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, it is also schedulable under a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive.

Proof. We first recall from Section III that the best-case schedulability condition is independent of the cyclic executive. To prove the lemma, we therefore only have to show that when the worst-case deadlines of S are met under a single-rate timedriven AFAP cyclic executives, these deadlines are also met under a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive. We now prove the lemma by deriving (2) from (4).

Theorem 5. (Theorem 3 in [8] without proof) From a scheduling perspective, the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive dominates the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive.
Proof. The result follows immediately from Lemma 5 and system S II .

In [8], OOA algorithms for a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive were not considered nor mentioned. In this paper, we proved that even when an OOA algorithm is applied for the single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive, the single-rate AFAP cyclic executive dominates the singlerate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive from a scheduling perspective.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper considered optimal order assignment (OOA) algorithms for a system S and a task set T S , scheduled using a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive. First, a proof was presented for a conjecture of a basic OOA algorithm in [9]. Next, an enhanced OOA (E-OOA) algorithm was presented, that not only determines an order assignment to make a system S schedulable, if such an order exists, but also the maximum cycle time for which S is schedulable. The E-OOA algorithm was proven and illustrated by means of an example system. Finally, a proof was presented for a theorem in [8] stating that a single-rate AFAP cyclic executive dominates a single-rate time-driven AFAP cyclic executive.

Topics of future work include refining the basic real-time system model by taking the notion of observable event [16] into account. The last observable event of a task (in our case a response) need not be the end of a task's execution. Moreover, a job of a task does not necessarily provide a response, i.e. without a detected event there will be no response. Hence, our basic real-time system model may be refined to take these two aspects into account.
